source_title: WAO & Resuscitation Council UK: Anaphylaxis Recognition, Intramuscular Epinephrine Delivery, and Post-Event Monitoring
issuing_authority: World Allergy Organization (WAO) & Resuscitation Council UK

chunks.section_header: Anaphylaxis Diagnostic Criteria and Immediate Intramuscular Adrenaline
chunks.text_content: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterized by rapid onset of airway, breathing, or circulation problems usually associated with skin or mucosal changes. Diagnostic criteria: Acute onset of illness (minutes to several hours) with involvement of skin/mucosal tissue (urticaria, generalized pruritus, swollen lips/tongue/uvula) PLUS at least one of: Respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia) OR Reduced blood pressure/end-organ dysfunction (syncope, incontinence, hypotonia). First-line treatment is IMMEDIATE intramuscular injection of epinephrine/adrenaline (1:1000 / 1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral mid-thigh: 0.5 mg in adults, 0.3 mg in children 6-12 years, 0.15 mg in children <6 years. Repeat every 5 minutes if no clinical response.

chunks.section_header: Patient Positioning and Biphasic Reaction Vigilance
chunks.text_content: Crucial clinical pitfall: Do not allow an anaphylaxis patient to stand or walk abruptly; sudden assumption of an upright posture has caused fatal pulseless electrical activity (empty heart syndrome) due to vena cava pooling. Keep the patient supine with lower extremities elevated, or semi-seated if severe respiratory distress predominates. Biphasic reactions (recurrence of anaphylaxis without allergen re-exposure) occur in up to 20% of cases, typically within 4-12 hours; thus, all patients receiving adrenaline must be transported to an emergency department and monitored for a minimum of 6 hours.
